headline: One worker with AI could do 10 jobs, Zoho founder warns of faster desk job cuts
summary: Zoho's founder warns that AI's rapid improvement makes job losses in computer-based work 'ever more real,' potentially leading to a painful transition as labor needs decrease faster than new demand emerges.
details: Zoho, a business software company, issued a warning on October 29th, stating that AI could enable one skilled office worker to perform the jobs of ten. This raises the risk of faster and more significant cuts to desk jobs.

In a post on X, the Zoho founder and chief scientist highlighted that the risk of job losses in computer-based work is "getting ever more real." This assessment comes as AI, software capable of generating text and analyzing data, continues to improve rapidly.

While Vembu did not predict a 90% disappearance of jobs, he emphasized that the transition could be painful. This is because lower labor needs may materialize faster than new demand for human work can be created.

The post, unusually blunt for a major software executive, framed AI less as a distant productivity story and more as an immediate labor shock for white-collar work. It underscored the urgency of addressing AI's impact on employment.

Vembu's clearest numerical statement was the 1:10 ratio, implying that companies could achieve the same output with far fewer people if they prioritize efficiency over headcount growth. This shifts the focus of AI policy from model safety to the speed at which employment adjusts to increased worker output.

Vembu argued that cheaper work, enabled by AI, could lead to lower prices and the creation of new businesses. These new ventures might absorb some displaced workers over time, offering a potential long-term rebalancing.
However, the core problem, he noted, is timing. If productivity jumps quickly and new demand takes years to catch up, the immediate impact will be felt first on wages, hiring, and entry-level jobs.

The attention garnered by Vembu's post reflects a significant shift in the AI conversation in 2026. Investors and executives are now discussing less about whether AI works, and more about the implications when it works well enough to automate routine desk tasks.

For companies, this puts existing hiring plans and training budgets under intense scrutiny as they adapt to new capabilities. For policymakers, it sharpens the difficult question of whether education and labor regulations can evolve as quickly as AI deployment.
